docs.text:
• Use the encoders: what the encoders arm gives your agent.
  • Datasets: which routes each dataset allows.

docs.title: Use the encoders
docs.text: For encoder users. You run Perception's gateway locally and call encoders over HTTP from your own code.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• MedOmni installed, and Docker.
  • Inputs in a supported family. Each encoder reads exactly one family; see Encoders and Families.
  • A GPU for some encoders. Each encoder's model card says what it needs.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Build the image of each encoder you need. The check builds it and runs it on the encoder's test data.

    medomni perception check perception/encoders/ecg-12lead-500hz-mv/ecgfounder

  2. Start the gateway on the built encoders, pointing it at the folder that holds your inputs. The folder is mounted read-only into every encoder container.

    medomni perception up --data-root ~/samples

    It listens on 127.0.0.1:8000.

  3. List the encoders and read a model card before you rely on an encoder.

    curl "localhost:8000/encoders?family=ecg-12lead-500hz-mv"

    curl localhost:8000/cards/ecg-12lead-500hz-mv__ecgfounder

  4. Send an input and read the evidence. The path is relative to the data root.

    curl -X POST localhost:8000/encode -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"encoder_id": "ecg-12lead-500hz-mv__ecgfounder", "path": "ecg/record.hea"}'

docs.title: Check
docs.text: A successful encode returns evidence: the encoder's outputs with their provenance, and the reliability and limits from the model card. The first call to an encoder waits for its container to start; the response reports the wait in runtime.container_start_ms. The request and response shapes are in Gateway API.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Encoders: the model card format and every encoder in this version.
  • Add an encoder: package a new encoder for a family.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
MedOmni v0.3.0 in five views:

  • the repository layout
  • who uses it (C4 C1)
  • its containers (C2)
  • the components inside the medomni package (C3)
  • C1 to C3 nested in one picture

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
The repository holds one package, medomni: Core and three projects. Code is under src/; content that people write and review (families, dataset packages, task templates, cohorts, benchmarks, agent configs, encoders) is in one top-level folder per project. The starting files that each new command writes are inside the package.

MedOmni/
├── src/medomni/
│   ├── core/                 medomni.core
│   │   ├── cli/              the medomni command
│   │   ├── contracts/        typed models, validators, schemas/
│   │   ├── plugins/          entry-point loading
│   │   ├── loading/          format readers (CSV, OMOP, folder trees, recording headers) and the loader
│   │   ├── families/         registry loader, converter interface, dummy-data generator
│   │   ├── cache/            cache backends, cache commands
│   │   ├── tasks/            built tasks: atom layout, task sets, checks, the atom's shared Harbor parts
│   │   ├── builders.py       TaskBuilder, the interface every task builder follows
│   │   └── testing/          runs the checks each project registers
│   ├── bench/                medomni.bench
│   │   ├── runs/             runner interface, Harbor runner (assets/harbor/), replay; run and prediction records
│   │   ├── arms/             the run side of the four built-in arms
│   │   ├── scoring/          scorer, behaviour metrics
│   │   └── metrics.py        auc, qwk, mae
│   ├── perception/           medomni.perception
│   │   ├── registry/         catalogue, image builds and pulls
│   │   ├── runtime/          serving code built into every encoder image
│   │   ├── gateway/          the HTTP service
│   │   └── sidecar/          the perception service: the gateway beside each atom task's agent
│   └── studio/               medomni.studio
│       ├── build/            the medomni-v1 builder: its recipe format, task steps, cohort selection, its checks, the arms' build side, config hashes
│       └── survey/, propose/, review/ (with the audit), preview/, assets/, report/
├── core/
│   └── families/             one file per family, and aliases.yaml
├── bench/
│   ├── benchmarks/<benchmark>/  benchmark.yaml (the card), sets/ (task sets: pinned <template>@<cohort> lists)
│   └── agents/               contributed agent configs
├── perception/
│   └── encoders/             <family>/<encoder>/: built into images, not installed
├── studio/
│   ├── datasets/<dataset>/   dataset package: dataset.yaml, labels.yaml, evidence.yaml,
│   │                         codes.csv, policy.yaml, hooks/, tasks/<template>/
├── tests/                    core/, bench/, perception/, studio/
├── docs/                     this site
└── pyproject.toml
  • One name per project. Its package, content folder, command and docs section use the same name: medomni.perception, perception/, medomni perception …, Perception.
  • Code and content are apart. A new dataset, task, family or encoder changes content only; the code that reads it is unchanged.
  • Projects depend only on Core. Bench and Perception never import each other. Studio may also import Bench and Perception; nothing imports Studio. They register their commands, checks, content kinds and audit checks with Core; see How Core finds the projects. Design principles gives the rules.
  • Studio builds, Bench runs and scores. They meet at the built-task contract, so Bench runs a task whoever built it, and runs and scores with Studio removed.
  • Core names no content. No dataset, benchmark, arm, runner or project folder is named in Core's code; MedOmni's own are the first of each kind, registered like any other.
  • One page per component. Core: Contracts, Built tasks, Families, Cache, Plug-ins. Bench: Runs, Scoring. Studio: Overview, Datasets, Tasks, Build, Recipes, Audit. Perception: Encoders, Gateway.

docs.title: Context (C1)
docs.text:
• Agent evaluator: describes an agent, builds a task set from their own data with Studio, runs the agent on it with Bench, reads the scores.
  • Encoder user: calls the encoders through Perception's gateway.
  • Contributor: adds an agent, a dataset, a task or an encoder through its extension point, and proposes and reviews tasks in Studio.
  • MedOmni: one package with one command, holding Core, Bench, Perception and Studio.
  • Plug-in packages: outside medomni-* packages that add agents, datasets, tasks or encoders without a pull request.
  • Datasets: MIMIC-IV, AI-READI and BDSP under your own license, and VitalDB, read from local disk.
  • Harbor: the agent-evaluation framework that runs each atom task in Docker.
  • Model provider: the API behind an agent's model on a cloud route. A local route needs none.
  • Container registry: where medomni perception pull pulls encoder images from (ghcr.io/medomni). Nothing is published there yet; images are built on your machine.
  • Hugging Face: model cards, and dummy data for each dataset. No real record is published there.

docs.title: Containers (C2)
docs.text:
Container Project Does medomni command Core The entrance: finds the projects through entry points and the plug-in packages' content folders and entry points, then hands each subcommand to its project. Workspace Core Configuration, the cache, built atom tasks, the run folders and the results file, on your machine. Never committed. Bench library Bench Checks built tasks, turns a task set into Harbor jobs, records runs and scores them. Perception service Bench Runs inside each atom task with encoders: Perception's gateway, with Bench's call budget, family filter and call log. Perception library Perception Builds and checks encoder images, and starts the gateway. Gateway Perception The HTTP service in front of every encoder: its catalogue finds encoders and serves model cards, its router sends each call to a running encoder container. Encoders Perception One image per encoder, each reading one family. Built on your machine; model cards on Hugging Face. Studio tools Studio Build atom tasks from your data with the medomni-v1 builder, survey datasets, collect and review task proposals, preview cohorts, run the audit and report results.

Gateway and encoder images are tagged with the MedOmni release that built them. The gateway runs any encoder image built since the Container API last changed.

docs.title: Components of the package (C3)
docs.text:
Project Component Module Does Core Command medomni.core.cli The medomni command. Finds each project's subcommands through entry points; see Commands. Core Contracts medomni.core.contracts The versioned formats, each with a typed model and a validator. See Contracts. Core Plug-ins medomni.core.plugins Finds the projects' entry points, and the plug-in packages' content folders and entry points. Core Testing kit medomni.core.testing Runs the checks each project registers. Plug-in packages import it for their own CI. Core Loading medomni.core.loading The format readers, and the loader that runs a dataset package through them into its event table. Core Families medomni.core.families The family registry, the converter interface and the dummy-data generator. Core Cache medomni.core.cache The cache backend call, the folder and none backends, and the cache commands. See Cache. Core Built tasks medomni.core.tasks, medomni.core.builders The atom layout, task sets, the checks on built tasks, and the TaskBuilder interface. See Built tasks. Bench Harness medomni.bench.runs The agent runner: turns a task set into Harbor jobs and records runs and prediction records. Bench Arms medomni.bench.arms The run side of the four built-in arms. The harness looks up any arm by its registered name. Bench Scorer medomni.bench.scoring Scores complete tasks from their prediction records, one score record per target. The only thing that writes scores. Perception Gateway medomni.perception.gateway The gateway service, built into the gateway image. Perception Registry medomni.perception.registry The encoder catalogue: model cards, images, pulls and the encoder check. Perception Perception service medomni.perception.sidecar The gateway beside each atom task's agent, with the call budget, family filter and call log. Bench starts it through medomni.services. Studio Build medomni.studio.build The medomni-v1 builder: its recipe format (task templates, cohorts, labels, evidence) and the engine that runs recipes into atom tasks, with the arms' build side and config hashes. See Build. Studio Tools medomni.studio One subpackage per tool kind: survey, propose, review (with the audit), preview, assets, report.

The projects meet in contracts: Studio's builder writes built tasks that Bench reads, and Bench starts Perception's perception service through the medomni.services entry point and talks to it only through the Gateway API. Bench imports no Perception code and no Studio code.

Contributors and plug-in packages add agents, datasets, tasks and encoders to the projects; Extend MedOmni lists each extension point with its template and check.

docs.title: How Core finds the projects
docs.text:
Core is the medomni command and the shared machinery. It imports no project; each project tells Core what it adds, through entry points in MedOmni's own pyproject.toml:

  • its subcommands, such as medomni bench …, in medomni.commands
  • the checks behind its check commands, and its audit checks, in medomni.checks
  • its content kinds, each a folder pattern and its contract, such as studio/datasets/*/dataset.yaml, in medomni.content
  • a service a run starts beside the agent, such as Perception's perception service, in medomni.services

This is internal wiring, done once per project. Users never do it; a later project joins the same way. Outside packages that add pieces use plug-ins instead.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Design principles: the principles behind this layout.
  • Reference: the contracts each project reads and writes.
  • Commands: every subcommand.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: The ideas behind MedOmni. Each entry links to the page with the details.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: Project A part of MedOmni with its own package, content folder, command and docs section. v0.3.0 has three: Bench, Perception and Studio. Bench and Perception depend on Core and not on each other; Studio may also use them. Core What every project uses: the contracts, the medomni command, plug-in loading, dataset loading, families, the cache, the built-task contract and the testing kit. Projects register with it; it imports none of them. Only the MedOmni team changes it. See Architecture. Bench The project that evaluates AI agents on medical tasks. It runs an agent on built tasks in Harbor, with or without encoders, and scores the answers, whoever built the tasks. See Test your agent. Studio The project that makes and builds tasks, and the work people do around Bench and Perception: dataset survey, task proposals, review and sign-off, cohort previews, MedOmni's task builder, the audit and reports. A proposal ends in a frozen task template, which the builder turns into built tasks. See Studio. Perception The project that turns medical data into evidence an agent can use. It serves the encoders through the gateway. See Use the encoders.

docs.title: Data and encoders
docs.text: Dataset A source of patient data, used under its own license: MIMIC-IV, AI-READI, BDSP or VitalDB. MedOmni ships no data. A dataset package, which is configuration only, says how to read it. See Datasets. Event table The table every dataset becomes: one row per event, with raw files as FILE//<family> rows. Every later step reads it. See Datasets. Family A declared input format, such as 12-lead ECG at 500 Hz. Datasets supply files in families; encoders read them. See Families. Encoder A containerised model or rule that reads one family and returns evidence: labels, events, text or embeddings, with their provenance and reliability. See Encoders. Gateway The HTTP service in Perception that lists encoders, serves their model cards and runs them. Agents and your own code call encoders through it. See Gateway.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Task template A clinical question with its targets, and an agent block with the agent's instruction and environment. A frozen template is the end of Make. See Tasks. Cohort A recipe next to a template: who is included, at which prediction time, and how many per class. A template and a cohort are written <template>@<cohort>, and are one task with a version N.X. See Recipes. Recipe The format MedOmni's builder, medomni-v1, reads for what it takes from a dataset: the cohort, the labels and the evidence. It holds rules, never patient ids. See Recipes. Build MedOmni's task builder, medomni-v1, in Studio: it turns a template, a cohort and your copy into atom tasks. See Build. Task builder Code that writes built tasks: a content folder with the answers, and one atom task per patient under each arm. Any builder that follows the built-task contract can feed Bench. See Built tasks. Atom task One patient's evidence and the question, at the patient's prediction time: the unit an agent runs. See Built tasks. Task set A published list of <template>@<cohort> pairs, each pinned at its version, and the arms to build them under. It is named <benchmark>/<set>, such as medomni-bench/v1. Scores are compared on task sets. See Tasks. Benchmark Several task sets under one card: version, owner, license and the intelligence kinds it accepts. MedOmni's own is medomni-bench; a plug-in package can publish another. See Tasks. Cache The results of slow steps, kept only to save time: a build with no cache gives the same atom tasks. See Cache. Intelligence The system being evaluated, with a kind. v0.3.0 has one kind, agent: a scaffold driving a model, described in an agent config. Records name it as intelligence: {kind, name}. See Runs. Arm One way of giving the same tasks to the intelligence, compared side by side, as in a clinical trial: with encoders, without them, or adding input families rung by rung. A builder implements what the arm hides or shows; Bench implements what the run attaches. See Runs.

docs.title: Extending MedOmni
docs.text: Contract A versioned format with the validator that checks it, such as the task template or the model card. Projects and plug-in packages depend only on contracts. See Contracts. Extension point A place where contributors add to MedOmni: an agent in Bench, a dataset or task in Studio, an encoder in Perception. Each has a new command that writes its starting files and one check command, and is filled by pull request or from a plug-in package. See Contribute.

docs.title: Extend MedOmni
docs.text: What you can add to MedOmni, how, and what checks it.

docs.title: Three ways in
docs.text:
• Use it as is. Your own agent config, your own data copy and your own code calling the gateway need no registration and no pull request.
  • Pull request. The piece joins MedOmni's repository and its releases.
  • Plug-in package. The piece stays in your own medomni-* package and loads like a built-in one. See Plug-ins.

docs.title: What you can add
docs.text:
You add Project Follows contract Create with Check Pull request Plug-in package An agent Bench Agent config medomni bench agent new medomni bench run --set medomni-bench/smoke-dummy bench/agents/ content folder: bench/agents/ A dataset Studio Dataset config, recipe, dataset policy medomni studio data new medomni studio data check openly licensed only content folder: studio/datasets/<dataset>/ A task Studio Task template, recipe medomni studio task new medomni studio task check openly licensed data only content folder: studio/datasets/<dataset>/tasks/<template>/ A benchmark Bench Benchmark card, task set bench/benchmarks/<benchmark>/ medomni studio task check --set <benchmark>/<set> MedOmni team only content folder: bench/benchmarks/<benchmark>/ An encoder Perception Model card, Container API medomni perception new medomni perception check perception/encoders/ content folder: perception/encoders/<family>/<encoder>/ An arm Bench, and each builder The arm interface A plug-in package medomni studio task build --set <benchmark>/<set>, on a set that lists it no: the four built-in arms are fixed entry points: medomni.arms, and medomni.arm_builds per builder A task builder Studio Built task, TaskBuilder A plug-in package medomni bench run --set <benchmark>/<set> on what it builds no: MedOmni's builder is medomni-v1 entry point: medomni.builders A cache backend Core The cache backend call A plug-in package medomni cache build <dataset> no: Core ships folder and none entry point: medomni.caches A Studio tool Studio Its kind's interface src/medomni/studio/<kind>/ medomni studio check src/medomni/studio/<kind>/ entry point: medomni.tools
  • Every check is the same in MedOmni's CI, in your terminal and in a plug-in package's CI (testing kit).
  • Add an encoder, Add a dataset, Add a task and Contribute walk through each one.
  • A benchmark is a card (version, owner, license, the intelligence kinds it accepts) and its task sets. MedOmni's own is medomni-bench; a plug-in package publishes its own the same way.

docs.title: What you can use without adding anything
docs.text: You use Through See Your own agent An agent config file on your machine Test your agent Your own data copy medomni bench data connect Connect your data The encoders from your own code The Gateway API Use the encoders Results in your own analysis The result records in the run folders and results.jsonl Test your agent

docs.title: What you ask the MedOmni team for
docs.text:
Open an issue for these. Only the MedOmni team changes them, because every project depends on them.

  • a new family, or a new alias for one
  • a new format reader, for a file format no format reader knows
  • a new shared code
  • a change to any contract

docs.title: Not open in v0.3.0
docs.text:
• Metrics. Targets use auc, qwk or mae.
  • Runners. The agent is the only kind of intelligence, and Bench's harness is its runner.
  • Other tool access. Inside an atom task the agent reaches only the perception service. Other tool access, such as MCP servers or skills, would be added beside it later, not inside it.

docs.title: Data governance
docs.text:
• Licenses. Every use of a dataset follows its license and data use agreement. Source data never leaves the machine that holds the access.
  • Derived data. Tasks, answers, traces and results built from a dataset count as patient data. They stay in the workspace. The repository holds only code, contracts, dataset packages, templates and recipes.
  • Policies. Each dataset has a policy read from its license. medomni bench run refuses a model route the policy does not allow.

docs.title: Task reproducibility
docs.text:
• Determinism. The same template and cohort on the same data build the same atom tasks, byte for byte.
  • Rules, not lists. Cohorts are published as recipes, never as lists of patients.
  • Verification. Anyone with the data can rebuild a task from its config. The config hash shows whether two results used the same config; it doesn't show they used the same data. A local copy that differs under the same release name isn't detected.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
The last column names the projects each principle comes from.

Principle In MedOmni Learned from One command Every user task is a medomni subcommand, grouped by project: medomni bench …, medomni perception …. Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench Projects in one repository Bench, Perception and Studio each have their own package under src/medomni/ and their own content folder. Bench and Perception depend only on Core; Studio may also use them. A project moves to its own repository, with its history, when it has its own owner, users and release schedule. HELM and MedHELM, PyHealth; MONAI and OpenMMLab, which merged repositories back Versioned contracts Projects and plug-in packages depend only on contracts. Contracts change only in a minor release, and files from the previous minor release still load. MONAI bundles, scverse AnnData, langchain-core, the Harbor task format Locked core Only the MedOmni team changes Core. Core imports no project; projects register with it through entry points. Contributors add agents, datasets, tasks and encoders, each started by a new command and checked by one check command. pytest and MkDocs plug-ins, OpenMMLab registries Plug-in packages An outside medomni-* package adds agents, datasets, tasks or encoders without a pull request, in a content folder laid out like the repository and read by the same loader. Tasks on data that cannot leave an institution join this way. HELM, Inspect, lm-eval-harness, Harbor registries Shared checks medomni.core.testing runs the same checks in MedOmni's CI and in a plug-in package's CI. langchain-tests, nf-core lint, MONAI bundle CI Harbor as the runner Bench runs agents on Harbor. Terminal-Bench Credit The history keeps each contributor's commits, with their author and date, and a CONTRIBUTORS file names everyone and what they built. Every model card and task template lists its authors. MONAI bundles, MTEB, Terminal-Bench

docs.title: Docs composition
docs.text:
• Plain language. Use the most direct word and the fewest words that state the fact. Avoid:
    • slogans and paired phrases ("one X, one Y")
    • contrasts set up for effect ("X, not Y")
    • modifiers that add no fact
  • Bullets. When content is a list of items, steps or facts, write short bullets, one point each. A bullet need not be a full sentence.
  • Necessary. Keep a line only if a reader needs it to use or understand MedOmni.
  • No overlap. Each fact lives on one page; other pages link to it.
  • Complete. Everything a user needs to run, read or extend this version is here.
  • Current terms. Use this version's terms, and the same term everywhere.
  • Minimal structure. Add a page only when no existing page can hold the content.

docs.title: Runs
docs.text:
A run is one agent on one atom task, once. Bench runs any built task, whoever built it. The harness turns a built task set into Harbor jobs, Harbor runs each atom task in Docker, and the harness records each run and its answers in the job's run folder.

agent config + built task set ──harness──▶ Harbor jobs ──▶ one run per atom task × arm × repetition
                                                     ├──▶ run records, in the run folder
                                                     └──▶ prediction records ──▶ scorer ──▶ results file

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
The system being evaluated is an intelligence. Its kind in v0.3.0 is agent: a scaffold driving a model, described in an agent config. The config names the kind, the agent, the model and the route (local or cloud); its settings, which the runner reads and checks, hold the scaffold (a Harbor agent such as terminus-2), the model name the provider must report back, and the run limits. Test your agent lists every field.

The replay agent repeats recorded runs with no model calls. MedOmni's own tests use it to run a task set at no cost.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
An arm is one way of giving the same tasks to the intelligence. Arms are compared side by side, as in a clinical trial. Bench has four:

  • encoders: with encoders
  • no-perception: without encoders
  • encoders-required: must call at least one encoder
  • modality-ladder: with encoders, at six rungs, r1 to r6; each rung adds input families to the one before

Every arm renders its own atom tasks from the same content, and each has its own config hash. A task set lists its arms, and the builder builds every pair under each of them.

  • encoders, no-perception and encoders-required differ only in encoder access and the instruction paragraph that describes it. Patients, files and answers are identical.
  • modality-ladder has its own ladder cohort, the same at every rung. Rungs differ only in the families staged. The rungs and their masks are in the template folder's arms/modality-ladder.yaml. Records name the rung in arm_variant.

An arm is one name, with a one-line description, registered in medomni.arms. It has two sides:

  • Build side: what it changes in the built atom task, such as the instruction paragraph, staged files or masks. Each builder implements it for the arms it supports, and refuses any other; the definition and variant are in the task's config hash.
  • Run side: what the run attaches, such as the perception service and its call budget. Bench implements it.

A plug-in package can add an arm: its run side in medomni.arms, and its build side for a builder in medomni.arm_builds as <builder>:<arm>, such as medomni-v1:my-arm. The harness reads an arm's variants from the built task's manifest. medomni bench run --arm <arm> picks the arms to run, and medomni plugins lists the arms plug-in packages add.

docs.title: Inside an atom task
docs.text:
• The agent works in a closed-network container with the patient's files.
  • When the arm attaches it (every built-in arm except no-perception), the perception service runs beside it, at http://perception:8899. It is Perception's gateway, which Bench starts and reaches only through the Gateway API. It adds:
    • a call budget per atom task
    • a family filter: only the families staged for that patient are listed
    • a call log, recorded with the run
  • The agent writes its answer to the submission path. A format check confirms the answer's shape; it never scores.

docs.title: The harness
docs.text:
medomni bench run:

  1. checks the whole set, and runs nothing if any check fails:
    • the checks on built tasks
    • the stand-in agents on each task
    • the agent's route against the policy of each dataset the tasks hold data from: a denied route refuses the run, and a conditional route prints the conditions you must meet
  2. checks that the perception service's image is on your machine, when the arm attaches it
  3. writes one Harbor job per arm (and rung) and repetition, with what the arm attaches, and runs them
  4. records each run: ids, the intelligence, the task version and config hash, served model, cost and errors; and, in the run's agent block, the arm and its variant, the encoders served (id and image digest), encoder calls and files opened
  5. reads the agent's answer from the submission path and writes one prediction record per target to the run's predictions.jsonl

Running it again resumes: atom tasks that already have a run are skipped.

docs.title: Run folders
docs.text:
Each Harbor job is one folder under the workspace's runs folder, named <set>--<agent>--<arm>[.<variant>]--r<rep>--<stamp>, with the / of the set's name written as ., such as medomni-bench.v1--my-agent--encoders--r1--20261109-142000/. It holds:

  • runs.jsonl: one run record per atom task
  • predictions.jsonl: the prediction records
  • encoder_use.jsonl, on an arm with the perception service: each encoder call's level
  • one folder per trial, as Harbor writes it

Harbor sets file permissions in the job folder, so runs must be on a file system that supports them, not exFAT. Set it in the workspace's workspace.yaml.

The harness is Bench's runner for agents, registered in medomni.runners. Every runner has the same three steps: prepare the tasks, run them, and collect the predictions and run records.

docs.title: Prediction records
docs.text: A prediction record is one answer for one target of one atom task: run_id, atom, target, value and intelligence. It is the only thing the scorer reads from a run. A value is a number, or a class label as text.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/bench/runs/: the runner interface, the agent runner on Harbor, the replay agent, and run and prediction records
  • src/medomni/bench/arms/: the run side of the four built-in arms
  • src/medomni/bench/runs/assets/harbor/: the Harbor runner's job config
  • src/medomni/bench/runs/routes.py: the route check
  • src/medomni/perception/sidecar/: the perception service, with its call budget, family filter and call log; Perception owns it
  • bench/agents/: contributed agent configs
  • your workspace: the run folders and the results file

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Test your agent: the agent config fields and the commands.
  • Scoring: how runs become scores.
  • Gateway: what the perception service runs.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
The scorer turns the runs of one built <template>@<cohort> into scores: one per target, for each agent, arm and repetition. A score record names its arm in arm, and the ladder's rung in arm_variant. It is the only part of MedOmni that writes scores.

prediction records of one <template>@<cohort> ──▶ compare with its answers ──▶ one score record per target

docs.title: How a score is made
docs.text:
1. Read the prediction records of every atom task for the <template>@<cohort>, agent, arm and repetition. The scorer reads nothing else from a run.
  2. Check the set is complete and consistent.
  3. For each target, compare the predictions with the answers, using that target's metric.
  4. Write one score record per target to the results file.

Scoring all atom tasks together, after all their runs finish, means no run sees the answers.

docs.title: Refusals and failures
docs.text:
• A <template>@<cohort> with missing patients is refused.
  • Runs that differ among themselves in config hash, served model or served encoders are refused.
  • Rows with different config hashes in one table are flagged configured differently. The flag never voids a score.
  • Each score record carries the task set's content hash. The table only puts scores with the same hash side by side.
  • An agent failure, such as no answer or a malformed answer, scores as chance.
  • An infrastructure failure refuses the score.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Each target in a template names its metric, a name registered in medomni.metrics. Bench registers three:

  • auc: binary targets
  • qwk: ordinal targets
  • mae: numeric targets

Each score record holds the scorer version, a hash of the metric code. medomni bench score --force rescores under the current version.

docs.title: Behaviour metrics
docs.text:
On an arm with the perception service, Bench measures how far the agent took each encoder answer, at three levels:

  • called: the call is in the perception service's call log
  • surfaced: a value from the answer appears in the agent's terminal output after the call
  • cited: a message from the agent names that value before it writes its answer

Whether an answer changed the prediction needs a paired run without it, so that level is reported as unmeasured. Every encoder counts, whether or not its family bears on the targets.

  • Each run record counts the agent's calls per encoder, in agent.encoder_calls.
  • The run folder's encoder_use.jsonl holds each call's level.
  • Each score record's encoder_use sums up its row: how many atom tasks called an encoder, the share that reached each level, over those atom tasks and over all of them, and the share of surfaced answers never cited.

docs.title: Stand-in agents
docs.text:
Before every run, medomni bench run scores two stand-in agents on each task, with no model calls:

  • one that answers every patient's true values must score perfectly: AUC 1, QWK 1, MAE 0
  • one that gives every patient the same answer, the best one without looking, must score at chance: AUC 0.5, QWK 0, and MAE equal to the answers' mean distance from their median

A task that fails either has broken answers or scoring, such as an answer for no atom task, and nothing runs. The problems name the task, target and both scores, never a patient's value.

docs.title: Results file
docs.text:
results.jsonl in your workspace holds the score records (kind: score). The run records (kind: run) stay in each run folder's runs.jsonl.

  • Only medomni bench score writes it.
  • Lines are never edited; for a repeated run_id, the latest line wins.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/bench/scoring/: the scorer, the behaviour metrics and the stand-in agents
  • src/medomni/bench/metrics.py: auc, qwk and mae
  • your workspace: results.jsonl

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Test your agent: the results file fields.
  • Tasks: where the metrics and answers come from.

docs.title: Built tasks
docs.text:
A built task is what a task builder writes and what Bench runs and scores. Its files follow one contract, so Bench runs a built task whoever built it. MedOmni's own builder, medomni-v1, is in Studio; a plug-in package can add another.

builder ──writes──▶ built task: content + atom tasks ──Bench checks, runs and scores──▶ results

docs.title: The files
docs.text:
A built task is one content folder and one atom task per patient under each arm, in the workspace's built-task folder:

atomtasks/
├── _content/<task>/
│   ├── content.json       version, targets (name, metric), atoms (atom, subject, prediction time)
│   ├── answers.csv        each patient's answer for every target: subject_id, target, value, metric
│   └── manifest.json      config_hash (one per arm and variant), builder (<name>/<version>)
└── <arm>/[<variant>/]<atom>/
    ├── task.toml          the atom's metadata: task, patient, arm, variant, prediction time, resources
    ├── instruction.md     what the agent reads first
    ├── data/              the patient's staged files
    ├── environment/       the closed-network containers: docker-compose.yaml, Dockerfile
    └── tests/
        ├── expected.json  the target names
        ├── format_check.py
        └── test.sh
  • Bench's runner and scorer read content.json, answers.csv and manifest.json, and each atom's tests/expected.json and tests/format_check.py. Harbor reads the rest of the atom.
  • The contract names only the fields Bench reads. A builder may add its own fields to content.json and manifest.json, such as medomni-v1's step counts and release.
  • The runner finds an arm's variants in the keys of manifest.json's config_hash, such as modality-ladder/r1.
  • answers.csv stays in the content folder. No atom task holds it.
  • Core supplies the atom's shared Harbor parts, the agent's Dockerfile, bootstrap.sh, format_check.py and test.sh, so every builder stages the same ones.

A builder may write more files of its own, such as medomni-v1's record.json for each patient. Bench never reads them.

docs.title: Checks on any built task
docs.text:
Bench runs these on the whole task set before every run, whoever built it. If any fails, nothing runs. MedOmni's builder runs them too, right after it writes.

  • Files present: the content folder and every atom task hold the contract's files, and their fields follow it.
  • No answers in an atom task: no atom folder holds answers.csv, content.json or a patient's record.json.
  • Format check works: each atom's format_check.py accepts a well-formed submission.
  • Nothing after the prediction time: every staged file the builder dated, in the atom's data/references.jsonl, is dated at or before the prediction time in task.toml.
  • Complete recordings: every staged WFDB header comes with its signal files and segments. This check reads your copy of the data.
  • Closed network: every container of an atom task is on one internal network, with no route out.

The checks that need the recipe or the source data, such as no answer in the evidence, belong to the builder. See Build for medomni-v1's.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
An arm is one name, registered in medomni.arms. Its two sides are apart:

  • Build side: what the arm hides or shows in the atom task, such as the instruction paragraph, the staged files or the ladder's masks. Each builder implements it for the arms it supports, and refuses an arm it doesn't support.
  • Run side: what the run attaches, such as the perception service and its call budget. Bench implements it.

An arm from a plug-in package registers its run side in medomni.arms and its build side for each builder in medomni.arm_builds, named <builder>:<arm>, such as medomni-v1:my-arm. See Arms.

docs.title: Write your own builder
docs.text:
A builder is a subclass of TaskBuilder, registered in the medomni.builders entry-point group:

Member Is name The builder's registered name, such as medomni-v1. version The builder's version. It goes into every config hash the builder writes. config_files(task, arm, variant) What the task's config hash covers under that arm and variant: files, or bytes, by name. build(tasks, arms, workspace) Writes each task's content folder and its atom tasks under each arm in the layout above, and returns the content folders. It refuses, naming the task, anything it cannot build, such as an arm it doesn't support.

The task id is a string the builder understands; for medomni-v1 it is <template>@<cohort>. Core knows nothing of recipes, templates or cohorts.

A task set names its builder in its builder field, and medomni studio task build --set <set> builds it with that builder.

MedOmni's tests build a dummy set with a builder from a test package, then run it with the replay agent and score it. A builder whose output passes the checks above runs in Bench the same way.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/core/contracts/built.py: the built-task files, as models
  • src/medomni/core/tasks/: the atom layout, task sets, the checks on built tasks and the atom's shared Harbor parts
  • src/medomni/core/builders.py: TaskBuilder and the medomni.builders group
  • your workspace: the built tasks

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Build: MedOmni's builder, step by step.
  • Runs: how Bench runs a built task.
  • Plug-ins: register a builder or an arm from a plug-in package.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
The cache keeps the results of slow steps, such as loading a dataset or converting a recording, so a later build can skip them. It only saves time. Deleting it loses nothing but time, and a build with no cache gives the same atom tasks as a build with one. Nothing checks, compares or publishes what it holds.

your copy ──step──▶ cache ──▶ later builds

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
A step is a function of its arguments: the dataset, the step's name and version, its parameters and its inputs. Inputs are raw files, each named with its identity: a hash of the file, or for a large recording a quick identity, its size and its first and last MiB. The result's key is built from those arguments alone, so a changed input, parameter or step version gives a new key.

Core's steps are events, the dataset's event table, and one convert-<converter> per family converter.

A cache backend has one call:

run(dataset, step, version, params, inputs, make) -> (result, created)

make writes the step's files into an empty folder. run returns a folder holding those files, made now or kept from before, and whether it made them. Callers read only that folder.

  • A step writes real files only, no links, so every backend works on any file system, exFAT included.
  • Build copies files from the cache into atom tasks. Atom tasks never link to the cache.
  • Cache contents are derived from patient data. They stay on your machine and are never committed, uploaded or shared.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
The workspace config's cache names the backend:

cache: /home/me/medomni/cache          # the folder backend, at this path
cache: {backend: none}                 # keep nothing between processes
cache: {backend: my-cache, path: …, options: {…}}   # a backend from a plug-in package
Backend Keeps folder (the default) Each result in its own folder, <path>/<dataset>/<step>/<key>/, with a CACHE.json of the step, version, parameters, inputs and row counts. A result is never changed; the old one stays until cache gc removes it. none Nothing between processes. Within one process a step with the same arguments runs once.

A plug-in package adds a backend in the medomni.caches entry-point group, with no change to Core. path and options are the backend's own.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Does medomni cache build <dataset> Loads the dataset's event table into the cache, ahead of a build. medomni studio task build does this too, when needed. medomni cache status Lists the results per dataset and step, with size and whether a current step uses them. medomni cache gc [--dry-run] Removes results no current step uses, and unfinished folders. --dry-run lists them first.

cache status and cache gc are features of the folder backend. A backend without them says so.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/core/cache/: the backend call, the folder and none backends, and the commands
  • the path in your workspace config: the folder backend's results

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Build: the steps that fill the cache.
  • Rebuild a task set: build a published task set from your own copy.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text: A contract is a fixed format plus the validator that checks it. Every file or message that passes between projects, between MedOmni and a plug-in package, or between MedOmni and you, has one. Each side can change its code without breaking the other.

docs.title: The contracts
docs.text:
Contract Describes Written by Read by Family registry The schema of a family file and of its aliases MedOmni team Studio, Bench, Perception Dataset config A dataset package: description, format readers, rules, named definitions (their form is the builder's), converters Contributors Studio Event table The table every dataset becomes, with its FILE rows Core's loader Studio Dataset policy What a dataset's license allows Contributors Studio, Bench Built task The content folder and atom tasks a builder writes. See Built tasks A task builder Bench Benchmark card One benchmark: name, version, owner, license, the intelligence kinds it accepts MedOmni team, plug-in packages Studio, Bench, you Task set <template>@<cohort> pairs pinned at version N, the arms to build them under, and the builder MedOmni team, plug-in packages Studio, Bench, you Config hash The hash of a task's config files under one arm A task builder Bench, you Agent config One intelligence of kind agent: name, model, route, and the settings its runner reads You, contributors Bench Model card One encoder Contributors Perception, agents Container API Requests between the gateway and an encoder image MedOmni team Perception Gateway API Requests to the gateway and the evidence it returns MedOmni team Bench, agents, your code Prediction record One answer for one target of one atom task: the only handoff from a run to the scorer Bench's agent runner Bench's scorer Result record One run, or one score for one target, naming its intelligence Bench You, Studio Workspace config Where your data copies, built tasks and results are kept, and which cache backend is used You Bench, Perception, Studio

The fields of each are on its Reference page. Family files themselves are content, written by the MedOmni team; only their schema is a contract.

docs.title: Studio's formats
docs.text:
Studio defines its own formats. medomni contracts check checks them, and reading checks them, as for Core's contracts. They are not Core's: the recipe format belongs to MedOmni's builder, medomni-v1, and another builder may read other files.

Format Describes Written by Read by Recipe A cohort with its task version and test patients, a label library and evidence rules Contributors medomni-v1 Task template One task: targets, input, and an agent block (statement, instruction, environment, submission path) Contributors medomni-v1 Dataset config, as medomni-v1 reads it The dataset config, with its named definitions written as cohort requirements Contributors medomni-v1 Task proposal One proposed task and its review state Clinicians, reviewers Studio

docs.title: How a file is checked
docs.text:
• Each contract is a Python class in medomni.core.contracts that lists its fields and their types.
  • A file is checked when it is read. If a field is missing or wrong, reading stops and names the field and the reason.
  • After that, code works with the checked object, never with the raw YAML or JSON. The object cannot be changed, so no step can alter a template halfway through a build.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Contracts follow the MedOmni release, such as v0.3.0. They have no version numbers of their own.

  • A contract changes only in a minor release (v0.3 to v0.4), never in a patch release.
  • Every change is listed in the changelog, with what to do about it.
  • Files from the previous minor release still load, with a warning.
  • Files that MedOmni writes, such as built tasks and result records, record the release that wrote them.
  • A plug-in package states the releases it works with in its dependencies, such as medomni>=0.3,<0.4.

Three things outlive a release, so each carries its own marker:

  • Config hashes start with the algorithm that made them, such as cfg1:, so published config hashes stay checkable after an upgrade.
  • Tasks carry their own version, N.X, so a task set stays comparable across releases.
  • Encoder images record the release that built them. The gateway runs any image built since the Container API last changed, so a release that leaves the Container API alone needs no rebuild.

Only the MedOmni team changes contracts. To propose a change, such as a new family, open an issue.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
medomni contracts check

It validates every contract file in the repository and in the installed plug-in packages. CI runs it on every pull request. Each check command (Commands) also runs the validators for the pieces it checks.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/core/contracts/: the classes and validators
  • src/medomni/core/contracts/schemas/: one JSON Schema per contract, for tools outside Python
  • src/medomni/studio/build/contracts/ and src/medomni/studio/schemas/: Studio's formats and their JSON Schemas
  • core/families/: the family files, which follow the family registry contract
  • studio/datasets/<dataset>/: the dataset packages, which follow the dataset config and dataset policy contracts, and medomni-v1's recipe format

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Families: the registry both projects share.
  • Extend MedOmni: what you can add, and the contract each piece follows.

docs.title: Families
docs.text:
A family is a declared input format, such as ecg-12lead-500hz-mv: a 12-lead ECG at 500 Hz in millivolts. Datasets supply files in a family; encoders read one family. The family is where Bench and Perception meet.

dataset ──event table──▶ FILE//F rows ──▶ encoders that read F
   └─ other format ──family converter──▶ files in F

docs.title: What a family declares
docs.text:
• Format: the file formats it accepts, such as EDF, WFDB, DICOM or a table.
  • Channels or roles: the exact montage, a channel count, or roles at least one channel must match.
  • Rate and units: the sampling rate and dominant unit, where they matter.
  • Type and range: the data type of the values and their plausible range, such as 50–100 for SpO2 in %. A file outside the range is rejected, which catches unit and scaling errors that would otherwise pass silently.
  • Read by: deep-encoder, rule-extractor, or direct (the agent reads the file itself).
  • Status: declared (shape known), supplied (measured on real data) or deprecated.

The id names these facts: modality, shape, rate and unit.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text: Real files rarely match a protocol exactly. aliases.yaml lists what each family also accepts, such as channel relabels and extra sampling rates. Aliases are strict: an unknown key, family or target fails the check.

docs.title: How the registry is used
docs.text:
• A dataset's event table names each raw file as a FILE//<family> row.
  • Build checks staged files against their family.
  • The dummy-data generator, medomni.core.families.dummy, makes files from each family's protocol. Datasets says how a dataset's dummy data is made.
  • An encoder's model card names its one family; the gateway filters encoders by family.
  • The runtime in every encoder image uses this module for aliases, labels and format checks.
  • Every family count in MedOmni comes from the registry.

A new family is added by the MedOmni team. Family files are content; only their schema is a contract.

docs.title: Family converters
docs.text:
Some datasets store recordings in a format no family accepts, such as BDSP's HDF5 files or VitalDB's .vital files. A family converter turns a file in one raw format into a file of one family. It may serve several families, one conversion each, and a family can have several converters.

  • Each recording is converted once and kept in the cache, under a key that covers the source file's quick identity (its size and its first and last MiB), the family, the converter's version, and the parts of the family's declaration and aliases the conversion reads: channels, roles and channel prefixes. A change to any of them converts again. A change to a family's rate, units, type or range does not.
  • Core holds the converter interface. A converter for one dataset's raw format lives in that dataset package and is declared in its dataset.yaml; one for a format many datasets share registers in medomni.converters.
  • BDSP's h5-to-edf converter turns a night into one family's EDF.
  • VitalDB's vital-to-wfdb converter reads a VitalDB .vital case with the vitaldb package. It writes WFDB for arterial pressure and central venous pressure, and EDF for ECG lead II (in µV), the pleth and capnography, the families whose first format is EDF. Each track is resampled to its family's rate, and the recording is cut at the end of the operation. The EDF files start at 2000-01-01 00:00:00, the start of the case.
  • A converter is deterministic: the same input gives the same bytes. It writes no wall-clock time into a file header, so a build with or without the cache gives the same files.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• core/families/: one <id>.yaml per family, plus aliases.yaml
  • src/medomni/core/contracts/schemas/: the schema both follow
  • src/medomni/core/families/: the registry loader, the converter interface and the dummy-data generator
  • studio/datasets/<dataset>/: a dataset's own converters

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Families reference: every field of a family file.
  • Encoders: what reads a family.

docs.title: Plug-ins
docs.text: A plug-in package is an outside Python package, named medomni-<name>, that adds agents, datasets, tasks, benchmarks, encoders, arms, task builders, Studio tools or family converters without a pull request. Use one when the work should stay in your repository, for example tasks on data that cannot leave your institution. Extend MedOmni compares it with the other ways to add things.

docs.title: Content folder
docs.text:
Agents, datasets, tasks, benchmarks and encoders are files. A plug-in package ships them in one folder, laid out like MedOmni's repository:

medomni_myname/content/
├── bench/
│   ├── agents/<agent>.yaml
│   └── benchmarks/<benchmark>/
│       ├── benchmark.yaml         the benchmark card
│       └── sets/<set>.yaml        its task sets
├── studio/
│   └── datasets/<dataset>/        dataset package, with hooks/ and tasks/<template>/
└── perception/
    └── encoders/<family>/<encoder>/
  • The package registers the folder with one entry point, in the medomni.plugins group.
  • MedOmni reads the repository first, then each plug-in folder, with the same loader. A piece in a plug-in folder works as it would in the repository.
  • Each project registers its content kinds with Core in medomni.content: a folder pattern, such as studio/datasets/*/dataset.yaml, and the contract its files follow. Core names no project folder of its own.
  • Finding the folder runs none of the package's code. Python in a dataset's hooks/ is imported only when a build uses it.
  • Moving a piece between a plug-in and the repository is a folder copy.

docs.title: Python pieces
docs.text:
Pieces that are Python code register one entry point each, in the group for their kind:

Group Registers Used by medomni.commands A top-level command The medomni command medomni.checks Checks for the testing kit The testing kit medomni.content A content kind: a folder pattern and its contract Core's loader and medomni contracts check medomni.converters A family converter for a format several datasets share Core's cache, for a builder medomni.builders A task builder Studio medomni.caches A cache backend Core's cache medomni.services A service a run starts beside the agent, such as Perception's perception service Bench's agent runner medomni.arms An arm by name, and what the run attaches Bench's agent runner medomni.arm_builds An arm's build side for one builder, named <builder>:<arm> That builder medomni.tools A Studio tool of one kind Studio medomni.runners The runner for one kind of intelligence Bench medomni.metrics A metric a target may name Bench's scorer
  • Bench, Perception and Studio register their own pieces in the same groups, such as Bench's four built-in arms and Studio's builder, medomni-v1.
  • In v0.3.0, medomni.runners and medomni.metrics hold only MedOmni's own pieces: the agent runner, and auc, qwk and mae.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A package with a dataset, a task and a converter lists two entry points in its own pyproject.toml:

[project]
name = "medomni-myname"
dependencies = ["medomni>=0.3,<0.4"]

[project.entry-points."medomni.plugins"]
myname = "medomni_myname:content"

[project.entry-points."medomni.converters"]
my-format = "medomni_myname.converters:MyFormat"

After pip install medomni-myname, its dataset and task appear in Studio's commands.

Install the package as a wheel or in editable mode. Zip installs are not supported: they give no real folder, so hooks cannot load.

docs.title: How MedOmni loads them
docs.text:
• Names. Each piece is named <package>:<name>, such as medomni-myname:my-task. Built-in pieces use the package medomni.
  • Collisions. A plug-in command that reuses a built-in command name is skipped with a warning, and the built-in runs. Two other pieces of one kind with the same name are both listed with an error, and neither is loaded.
  • Lazy loading. At start, a command reads entry-point names and folder paths only. A piece is read or imported when a command first uses it.
  • Validation. Each piece is checked against its contract when it is read. A piece that fails is listed with its error and not used.
  • Same as built-in. A loaded piece works in every command as a built-in piece does.
medomni plugins

It reads every installed piece, checks it, and lists each package with what it adds and any errors.

docs.title: The testing kit
docs.text:
medomni.core.testing runs the same checks as MedOmni's CI. A plug-in package runs them in its own CI, so it passes the same checks as a pull request.

A plug-in's CI checks out MedOmni and installs it in editable mode (uv pip install -e .). MedOmni reads its built-in content (families, and Bench's, Perception's and Studio's content) only from a clone; outside one, it reads only plug-in folders.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/core/plugins/: finding content folders and entry points
  • src/medomni/core/testing/: the check runner

docs.text:

  • Contribute: publish a plug-in package step by step.

docs.title: Encoders
docs.text:
An encoder is a containerised model or rule that reads one family and returns evidence. Each encoder is one folder in the repository, built into one image, and described by one model card.

perception/encoders/<family>/<encoder>/ ──build──▶ image on your machine
                         card.yaml ──publish──▶ model card on Hugging Face

docs.title: The encoder folder
docs.text:
perception/encoders/<family>/<encoder>/
├── adapter.py      load() once, then encode(sample, options)
├── card.yaml       the model card
├── Dockerfile      pinned base image, dependencies, source revision
├── assets.json     weights and other files the image build fetches, each with its source and sha256 (if any)
└── testdata/
    ├── input.*         synthetic or openly licensed, written by medomni studio testdata
    ├── expected.json   the recorded responses, written by --freeze
    └── PROVENANCE.md   written by medomni studio testdata

The runtime in src/medomni/perception/runtime/ is built into every image. It declares the encoder interface, load and encode, and serves it through the container API. It reads each family's files with one decoder per family, and uses Core's families module for aliases, labels and format checks.

An encoder author writes only load and encode; the check fails an adapter that does not implement them. Everything else is shared by every encoder: asset preparation from assets.json, which the image build runs (five encoders instead fetch their weights with their own fetch_assets.py during the build); the encoder tests in tests/perception/; and two Studio tools, medomni studio encoder-demo and medomni studio testdata.

docs.title: Model card
docs.text:
The model card states an encoder's facts:

  • the family it reads and the outputs it returns: labels, events, text or embedding
  • where it comes from: source, weights, license
  • its intended use and known limits
  • whether it runs zero-shot, with no training on MedOmni data
  • its reliability: unmeasured or measured, with evidence

Agents read the card through the gateway before they rely on an encoder.

docs.title: Check and freeze
docs.text:
medomni perception check perception/encoders/<family>/<encoder>

It runs six stages in order and stops at the first failure:

  1. Card: validates the model card, as medomni contracts check does, and the folder.
  2. Dockerfile: before anything is built, every torch== install must use the listed build index and a listed version.
  3. Build: builds the image.
  4. Image torch: the torch installed in the image, if any, must be the listed build (+cpu) at a listed version. A dependency can bring in torch without any Dockerfile line naming it.
  5. Test data: runs the image on testdata/ and compares the responses with expected.json.
  6. Real samples: runs the image offline on real samples of its family and checks each response against the model card. It needs at least three, in --samples <dir>, such as the files medomni studio family-samples writes from your own copy of a dataset. MedOmni publishes no real samples. Without them, the stage reports UNVERIFIED-no-samples, or UNVERIFIED-access-controlled for a family whose real samples are access-controlled, and the test data stands in.

The list for stages 2 and 4 is src/medomni/perception/registry/torch.yaml: the CPU build index and the torch versions encoders pin. Images are CPU builds because the GPU build is about 5 GB larger, and the deployment, not the image, decides the device. A host that wants another build, such as CUDA, ships its own perception/torch.yaml in one plug-in content folder, which replaces the list. Two content folders that ship one are refused.

Stages 5 and 6 run the encoder's tests in tests/perception/. --freeze records expected.json from the current build; a later change that alters the responses fails stage 5.

--record writes an encoder that passed into perception/deployed.yaml, which pins the image the perception service starts for each encoder. It refuses an image built from uncommitted source, and leaves the other encoders' entries as they are, except that it drops an entry whose encoder has no folder in the repository or any plug-in content folder. The service serves an encoder whose entry passed stage 5 and did not fail stage 6. --record and --freeze can't be combined.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
• One image per encoder, built on your machine by medomni perception check, tagged ghcr.io/medomni/<encoder>:dev. MedOmni doesn't publish encoder images yet, so medomni perception pull has nothing to pull.
  • In a Bench run, the perception service starts only the image perception/deployed.yaml records for an encoder, by content id. Record your build with --record, then build the service image, which carries the record.
  • Users run images; they never install encoder code.
  • Licenses differ; the Encoders reference lists each one.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• perception/encoders/<family>/<encoder>/: each encoder
  • src/medomni/perception/runtime/: the serving code shared by every image, with one decoder per family in decoders/
  • src/medomni/perception/registry/: the catalogue, image builds and pulls, and torch.yaml, the torch builds an image may install
  • perception/deployed.yaml: the images the perception service starts, written by --record
  • tests/perception/: the encoder tests the check runs

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Encoders reference: model card fields and every encoder in this version.
  • Gateway: how encoders are found and called.
  • Families: what an encoder reads.

docs.title: Gateway
docs.text:
The gateway is one HTTP service in front of every encoder. Through it, an agent or your own code finds encoders, reads their model cards and runs them. It only finds, describes and runs encoders: the agent decides which to call and how to combine their evidence.

It has three parts:

  • Catalogue: finds encoders and serves their model cards.
  • Router: sends each call to a running encoder container.
  • Evidence: builds the answer and its fingerprint.
caller ──GET /encoders, /cards──▶ catalogue (no containers needed)
caller ──POST /encode──▶ router ──▶ encoder container ──▶ evidence

docs.title: Catalogue
docs.text:
Model cards are files, so the gateway loads every card at start. Searching and reading cards start no containers.

  • GET /encoders searches by text, family, modality, output kind or label.
  • GET /cards/{encoder_id} returns one model card.
  • GET /families lists each family with its encoder count.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
POST /encode sends one input to one named encoder. Only this call uses a container. For each call the router:

  1. Looks up the encoder in the catalogue. An unknown encoder, or one with a model card but no image, is refused.
  2. Checks its cache. An identical earlier request is answered from the gateway's own cache, in memory, without a container. The cache lasts while the gateway runs.
  3. Picks a container:
    • a running one for that encoder, if it is under its concurrency limit
    • otherwise a new one, if the pool is under its limit of live containers
    • otherwise it stops the least recently used idle container and starts a new one
    • otherwise it waits; one encoder is never started twice
  4. Sends the request to the container through the Container API.
  5. Handles failure: a container that fails or hangs is taken out, so the next call gets a fresh one.

Calls to several encoders are separate requests and run side by side, within the limits. A busy container is never stopped, and idle containers stop after a timeout.

The router routes by name only. Choosing encoders is the agent's job, and Bench's behaviour metrics measure that choice.

The response reports the start time in runtime.container_start_ms.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
Each encode returns evidence:

  • the encoder's outputs, unchanged
  • provenance: hashes of the input, weights and image
  • the reliability and limits from the model card
  • a fingerprint of encoder, weights, image, input and options

Evidence contains only the model card and the container's reply. Identical requests give identical fingerprints and are served from the cache.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
medomni perception up --data-root <dir>

It reads inputs from your data root, mounted read-only. Inside an atom task, Bench runs the gateway as the perception service, adding a call budget, a family filter and a call log. The gateway itself has none of these.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text: • src/medomni/perception/gateway/: the service, built into the gateway image

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:

  • Use the encoders: start the gateway and call it.
  • Runs: how Bench uses the gateway inside an atom task.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
The audit checks MedOmni's claims against its files, code and runs. Each part makes claims:

  • a family claims what its files contain
  • a model card claims what an encoder does
  • a task claims its answer is not in its evidence
  • a run claims it used the task and model it names

docs.title: Assets and criteria
docs.text:
The audit covers five assets: data, families, encoders, tasks and runs. Each is checked on four criteria:

  • Completeness: every required part is present.
  • Conformance: it matches its contract.
  • Isolation: no answer reaches the evidence, and no encoder has seen the evaluation data.
  • Clinical validity: the target means what it says.

The Audit reference shows which auditor covers each asset and criterion.

docs.title: Auditors
docs.text:
• Machine checks run on every audit and can only reject. For tasks, they read the results of Build's correctness checks, which refuse a bad task at every build. They add seven of their own: a test case for every leakage rule, the canary, the call budget, encoder limits, family coverage, the file inventory and the instruction.
  • LLM reviews are advisory.
  • Human sign-offs are required for clinical validity.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Machine checks only reject. Passing all of them means no contradiction was found.
  • A verdict binds to the asset's config hash (for a task: its template, cohort, labels, recipes and dataset release). After any of these changes, its LLM or human verdict reverts to unassessed.
  • Only threats to the main claim fail. An item fails if the answer is reachable in the evidence, an encoder has seen the evaluation data, or a target does not mean what it says. Other failed checks are warnings with their reason.
  • Patient-level traces never go to an LLM. Checks that need them are left for a human and reported as unassessed.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
medomni studio audit

It runs the machine checks, reads the recorded verdicts and writes a report and a findings list to the workspace.

docs.title: Release check
docs.text:
medomni studio release-check

It checks that the release tree may be published, before every release. It reads four things and fails on any conflict:

  • Encoder licences: every model card states a licence, and every built image carries the same one in its org.medomni.license label, which medomni perception check sets. An encoder under a restricted licence ships like the rest, with the licence stated on both. --no-images skips the labels, so the check runs without Docker.
  • Dataset publish rules: every file under a dataset package is a kind its policy's publish rules name and allow: schema files, templates or recipes. Any other file is refused.
  • Data files: every signal, image or array file sits in a folder, or the folder above it, with a PROVENANCE file that states a licence. Site images under docs/ aren't data.
  • Task set versions: the version check of medomni studio task check --release.

The release tree is the repository's tracked files, less the folders that stay private.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/studio/review/: the matrix, the runner and the report writer
  • each project's audit checks, registered through Core's plug-in loading: data and tasks from Studio, runs from Bench, encoders from Perception

docs.text:

  • Studio: the other review tools.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Build is MedOmni's task builder, medomni-v1, in Studio. It turns a task template, a cohort and your copy of a dataset into built tasks, which Bench runs and scores. It runs the same way on every machine, and the same inputs give the same atom tasks, byte for byte.

template + cohort + your copy ──Build──▶ content + step counts ──▶ atom tasks per arm + config hash

medomni studio task build runs it. The template, cohort, label and evidence files it reads are this builder's own format; another builder can read other inputs, as long as it writes the same built-task files.

docs.title: Make and Build
docs.text:
Make Build Part of Studio Survey, proposals, review The medomni-v1 builder Who People: dataset survey, clinician input, review No one: it runs alone Ends in A frozen task template and its cohorts Atom tasks and their config hashes Same result every time No Yes

A template only reaches Build once Make is done. Build never asks a question and never changes a template.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Loading runs once per dataset and is kept in the cache. The task steps run for each <template>@<cohort>.

Loading (from the dataset package):

  1. Verify: the copy is the dataset version the package describes, and every file it lists exists.
  2. Read: the format readers read the tables and files the package names, and only those.
  3. Rules: the package's timing and visit rules are applied.
  4. Write: the result is the dataset's event table.
  5. Check: one row per event, every code in the dataset's code list, every FILE path present.

Family conversion: each file in a format no family accepts is converted once by a family converter.

Task steps (from the recipe):

  1. Source population: the patients the cohort may select from, chosen by a hash rule.
  2. Prediction time: each patient's anchor event and offset.
  3. Requirements: the events and files each patient must have, in their windows.
  4. Labels: each target's answer, from the dataset's label library.
  5. Cohort selection and file check: the patients are ranked by hash within each class and taken from the top until each class has its share. When the cohort requires files to convert (converts), each patient's files are converted and checked against their families on the way down, and a patient whose files fail is replaced by the next one in rank. The patients selected are the ones a check of the whole pool would give; only their files are converted.
  6. Evidence: for each patient, the whole record up to the prediction time, minus the guards of every target. A file with no time of its own that holds later rows is cut at the prediction time when its family is listed in the evidence rules' files.crop.
  7. Content: written once per task: the atom list, the answers, the targets and scoring, and for each patient record.json, the evidence the instruction shows. The content checks run on it.
  8. Render: one atom task per patient under each arm the task set lists, with the patient's files staged from the cache and what the arm adds or masks. The answers are never copied in.
  9. Check: the atom tasks pass the checks on built tasks, and the config hashes and step counts are written to the build manifest.

Build stops, and names the step, when the recipe needs a kind of time the dataset does not have, such as hours on a dataset with visit dates only, or when a correctness check fails.

docs.title: Correctness checks
docs.text:
Build runs medomni studio task check on what it builds and writes no task that fails a check. It stops and names the check and the target or patient. The content checks read the recipe and the source data, so they are this builder's own. The atom task checks are Core's checks on built tasks, which Bench runs again before every run.

Content checks, after the content step:

  • No answer in the evidence: no row or file of a patient's evidence holds a target's answer or a field its label guards.
  • Eligible at the prediction time: each patient meets the cohort's requirements at the prediction time, such as an admission that is still open.
  • Events still ahead: for an event target, no positive patient's event is at or before the prediction time.
  • Enough patients: each target cohort selection balances on (select.by) has at least 5 selected patients in each class, or at least 2 distinct values if it is numeric. Any other target that falls short is marked in the content and left out of scoring.
  • Answers that vary: a target's answers over the source population are not all the same. If they are, the whole task is refused, and its cohort or target must change.

Atom task checks, after rendering: Core's checks on built tasks, such as no answers in an atom task, no image after the prediction time, complete recordings and a closed network. For a film to be checked, Build's image hook dates every film it stages.

Dataset check, in medomni studio data check:

  • Every label value classified: each raw value a label reads is classified in the dataset's label library.

docs.title: Config hash and step counts
docs.text:
• The config hash of each task under each arm covers its config files, the builder's name and version, and the releases, never data. The algorithm is in Tasks reference.
  • The step counts are the number of patients left after each task step, from the source population to cohort selection. With a file check, file check tried counts the patients whose files were checked, and file check counts the eligible patients less those that failed; the pool before cohort selection is the eligible patients, not yet confirmed to convert. They show where two builds of one task part ways: the build manifest stays local, and two people can compare their counts by hand.

Both are written to the build manifest, and both are hashes and counts only.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
The evidence of each patient is the whole record up to the prediction time, minus the guards of every target. The template's input and exclude do not narrow it: they record what the task's proposal asked for.

v0.3.0 builds one evidence variant, default. Build refuses a pair written <template>:full@<cohort>.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• src/medomni/studio/build/: the medomni-v1 builder: its recipe format and engine, the steps, cohort selection, its checks, the arms' build side and the config hash
  • your workspace: the cache and the built atom tasks

docs.text:
